Ports & Processes in the Inspector

Features·seedling·proposed·JUL 24, 2026

Live listening ports and the process tree for every terminal — one-click open, ssh-tunneled remote ports, forward management, and kill.

Contents

  • The panel and its flows
  • Detection: one scan on the owning host
  • Tunnels: reaching a remote port
  • Build plan — the PT track
    • PT1 — detection, sections, kill (one PR)
    • PT2 — remote forwards + management (one PR)

Agents constantly start dev servers, and the URL scrolls away into the scrollback. Kolu already knows everything around the server — cwd, git, agent state, the foreground command — but not the one fact you act on: where is the thing the agent just ran? This feature adds two live Inspector sections per terminal, inspired by kero.shKero shows child processes with CPU% / memory plus listening ports. We deliberately drop CPU% and memory: they duplicate btop, and CPU% is the most expensive part to build (stateful two-sample jiffies delta, per platform) for the least payoff. Kolu’s version keeps the actionable halves — ports you can open and processes you can kill.: Ports (listening TCP ports owned by this terminal’s process subtree, each one openable in a click — tunneled over ssh when the terminal lives on a remote host) and Processes (the shell’s live child tree, name + pid).

The panel and its flows

PORTS 3
🌐 5173 node ⤴ open ⇄ :61000 ⨯
🌐 9229 node ⤴ open
🌐 61922 workerd ⤴ open
＋ Forward a port…
PROCESSES 3
● bun 30587
● node 30588 ⨯ kill
● workerd 30596
FORWARDED PORTS — host pu-dev
⇄ 5173 → :61000 · auto · ⨯   ⇄ 8080 → :61003 · manual · ⨯

All rows update live off the terminal’s metadata; actions appear on hover, matching the existing Inspector sections in packages/client/src/right-panel/MetadataInspector.tsx.

  • Open, local terminal. Click a port chip → window.open("http://localhost:5173", "_blank", "noopener,noreferrer") — the same external-open idiom the Code tab uses (CodeTab.tsx:1114). New browser tab; an embedded in-kolu preview is deliberately deferred to PT3.
  • Open, remote terminal. Click → the client calls forwards.create { host, remotePort } → the server adds a local forward on the live ControlMaster connection and returns the local port → window.open("http://localhost:61000"). The chip stays labeled with the remote port and gains a ⇄ :61000 tunnel badge. Forwarding is lazy — on first click only, never eager for every detected port.An agent session can hold six listening ports (workerd spawns several); auto-tunneling all of them VS-Code-style keeps idle tunnels alive for ports nobody opens. The cost of lazy is one ssh -O forward round-trip (~milliseconds on the multiplexed socket) on first click.
  • Manage forwards. A Forwarded Ports group (host-scoped, shown when any forward is active) lists every tunnel for the active host — remote port, local port, origin auto (chip click) or manual — each with a cancel ⨯. Auto forwards self-cancel when the scanner sees the remote port disappear; manual forwards persist until cancelled or the host disconnects. All forwards die with the ControlMaster connection, so a dropped host can never leak tunnels.
  • Manual forward. The ＋ Forward a port… row (and a ⌘+K command Forward a port…) accepts a remote port number and creates a manual forward — for a port the scanner missed or one outside this terminal’s subtree.
  • Kill. Hover a process row → ⨯ kill sends SIGTERM via a terminals.killProcess { terminalId, pid } surface procedure; a port row’s ⨯ kills the owning pid (“free this port”). The server re-verifies, at signal time, that the pid still sits in that terminal’s subtree and still bears the same process name — a recycled pid is refused, never signaled.
  • Discoverability. One tip in settings/tips.ts: “Click a port in the Inspector to open the server an agent just started.”

Detection: one scan on the owning host

Process facts belong to the PTY owner, so the scanner is a new module in kaval — packages/kaval/src/processScan.ts — beside the existing foreground sampler (ptyHost.ts:620). One host-wide pass every 5 secondsThe cadence and the unref’d non-overlapping poll shape copy packages/padi/src/memorySampler.ts and its derived.cell(source({ read, install: everyMsOr(…) })) wiring in servePadi.ts:247. covers all PTYs at once — build the full pid→ppid table, partition it into per-shell subtrees, join listening sockets against each subtree:

  • linux — walk /proc/*/stat for the pid/ppid/comm table; read /proc/net/tcp + /proc/net/tcp6 for LISTEN rows and join their socket inodes against /proc/<pid>/fd readlinks. This is the same technique surface-daemon-supervisor/src/socketHolder.ts:100 already uses for unix sockets — mimic its structure.
  • darwin — ps -axo pid,ppid,comm for the table; lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -P -n -F pcn for ports, run under a hard timeout and SIGKILLed if wedged, exactly as socketHolder.ts:157 does. Both platforms gate CI, so the darwin path is day-one work, not a fallback.

Results publish per-PTY on the ptyHostSurface contract (like foreground samples), deduped by structural equality before publishing so an unchanged scan emits nothing — the churn guard that keeps a 5-second ticker from thrashing SolidJS. From there every layer exists: the padi sensor set folds the sample into TerminalSnapshot (two new schema entries in packages/terminal-vocab/src/schema.ts beside ForegroundSchema:145 — ProcessInfo { pid, name } and PortInfo { port, pid, name }), the surface serves it (snapshot-then-deltas invariant applies, per .claude/rules/streaming.md), and the client’s reconcile-backed store in useTerminalMetadata.ts:180 delivers leaf-grained ticks to the two new <Section> blocks.

Architecture verdict, conditioned on this build: the scanner is a leaf module inside kaval, not a @kolu/* package — precisely because it is a bounded, one-shot scan (read, join, return) with kaval as its only consumer. It is the choice of “one dumb pass per tick, no streaming, no watchers” that makes the verdict “leaf”; if it ever grows an independent consumer or its own reconnect/streaming volatility, re-run the three electricity tests and graduate it.

Tunnels: reaching a remote port

Detection on remote hosts is free — the scan runs inside the remote’s own padi and the new snapshot fields ride the existing ssh surface mirror. Reaching the port is the one new mechanism: a dev server on the remote is bound to 127.0.0.1 there, so the click needs an ssh local forward. Kolu already holds a persistent multiplexed connection per host (packages/surface-remote/src/controlMaster.ts — ControlMaster=auto on a kolu-private ControlPath), and OpenSSH mutates forwards on that live socket without a new handshake:

ssh -O forward -L 61000:127.0.0.1:5173 <host>   # add — ~ms, no auth prompt
ssh -O cancel  -L 61000:127.0.0.1:5173 <host>   # remove

The forward manager — packages/surface-remote/src/portForward.ts — lives in surface-remote because that package already owns the ControlMaster volatility; the module holds the (host, remotePort) → localPort map, picks a random free local port per forward, and exposes three things on the per-host surface: forwards.create, forwards.cancel, and a forwards cell (the list the Forwarded Ports UI renders). Local terminals bypass the manager entirely.This is the mechanism VS Code Remote-SSH uses for its port forwarding, so the ergonomics are well-trodden — including HMR websockets, which tunnel fine because the forward terminates at the remote sshd and connects out to remote-127.0.0.1.

PT1 — detection, sections, kill (one PR)

Scanner module + schema fields + sensor fold + the two Inspector sections + terminals.killProcess + the tip. Done when an e2e scenario runs node -e 'require("http").createServer((_,r)=>r.end("ok")).listen(8123)' inside a real kolu terminal and asserts the 8123 chip appears in the Inspector within two scan ticks, clicking it opens localhost:8123, and the kill action terminates the listener (chip gone next tick). The criterion pins the real path — kaval scan → ptyHostSurface → padi snapshot → surface → reconcile store — a client-side mock cannot satisfy it. Parser unit tests run against fixture /proc trees and fixture lsof -F pcn output, and the darwin CI gate (aarch64-darwin) must be green, not skipped.

PT2 — remote forwards + management (one PR)

Forward manager, forwards.* surface members, tunnel badges, Forwarded Ports group, manual forward input, ⌘K command. Done when, verified with the remote-host-testing harness against a real remote box: clicking a remote terminal’s chip creates the forward via ssh -O forward on the existing ControlMaster socket (the controlOptPairs path — a second ssh connection does not satisfy this), curl localhost:<localPort> returns the remote server’s body, cancelling the row makes that curl fail, and killing the host connection leaves no listener behind. Evidence video of the click-to-page flow per the evidence skill.

PT3 — embedded preview (deferred)

Open the forwarded page inside kolu — a browser pane in the Code tab, in the spirit of the Codex desktop app — instead of a new tab. Explicitly out of scope until PT2 shipsIt is a genuinely bigger build: a cross-origin iframe surface for arbitrary dev servers, and any server sending X-Frame-Options: DENY / frame-ancestors refuses to be framed, so the new-tab path must remain the fallback regardless.; no design here yet — when it matures this section is rewritten, not layered.
